messages.subject: optimizing analysis through vectorization of the multi_normal probability function
parts:
Hi stan users,

I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.

The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like

 
loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);

where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:

for (n in 1:N) {
        loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
}

However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:

Mu=X*Beta;

But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:

row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...

keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):

for(n in 1:N){
        Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
      } 

But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?

My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:

Mu=X*Beta;
"some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L); 

Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?

I'd really appreciate any input on this

Sincerely,
Martin

messages.subject: Re: optimizing analysis through vectorization of the multi_normal probability function
parts:
Hi again!

I now realize I posted my questions slightly prematurely! After digging more into the Stan manual (I truly recommend this, it is super!!) I realized that the vectorization was not the solution but reparameterization was! I had already done some reparameterizations in other parts of my code but I hadn't still managed to do any reparameterization to the multi_normal. On pages 234-235 I found (and finaly understood) a thorough description of how to reparameterize the multi_normal such that the multi_normal probability function was not needed but could be replaced by a standard normal and some fancy transformations in the transformed parameter block.

Following these descriptions resulted in no more divergent transitions, and I could very well use matrix algebra to form Mu, i.e. all problems went away!
SInce the description can be easily found in the manual (Modeling Language User's Guide and Reference Manual, Version 2.12.0 ) I refrain from posting my final code here. If anyone happens to find themselves having similar problems as the above I will be happy to answer questions (within the limits of my rudimentary knowledge about these issues...)-

Thanks to the authors of the Stan manual. Outstanding work! And thanks also to the authors of Stan! 

Sincerely,
Martin

row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...

keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):

      }

Daniel,
Sorry for late reply.
I'm not exactly sure I understand and can produce what you're asking for and maybe I'm totaly off here...apologies in that case!

Anyway, I assume you want the n_eff per the time it took for the chains to run (and I have seen in some places that this is an important "efficiency" measure).
I also assume you want some average over all parameters and that you want me to compare these measure between models run using the "normal" multinormal version and using the reparameterized version.

A slight complication is that my modelling is more complex than it might have seemed in my original post. 
I ran several versions of prior specifications for Sigma or its cholesky decomposition as I've seen in various places that this might afftect the results
(N.B. I'm by far not an expert on this, I've just read what more knowledgeable people have written,
e.g. Matt Simpson http://www.themattsimpson.com/2012/08/20/prior-distributions-for-covariance-matrices-the-scaled-inverse-wishart-prior

and Ignacio Alvarez http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014arXiv1408.4050A):

 

 a) inverse-Wishart (IW),
Σ~IW(nspecies + 1, ID)
 b) scaled inverse-Wishart (SIW),
  Σ=Δ Q Δ, Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); (∆)_ii=ξ_i  (Δ is a diagonal matrix); ξ_i~HalfN(0, 2)
 c) using the "separation strategy" of Barnard et al 2000 (Statistica Sinica) with inverse Wishart (SSIW),
 Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R=Δ_q Q Δ_q;  (Δ_q )_ii=1/√(Q_ii )(Δ_q is a diagonal matrix); Q~IW(nspecies + 1, ID); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5) 
 d) using the "separation strategy" with LKJ priors for the covariance/correlation (SSLKJ),
 Σ=Δ R Δ; (∆)_ii=σ_i (Δ is a diagonal matrix); R~LKJ(1); σ_i~HalfCauchy(0, 5)


The "effect" of reparameterization differs somewhat between these versions.

Note also that I set adapt_delta to different values in the two model versions...

Anyhow, this is what I did and can report (I work in R using rstan):
For each stanfit I extracted the summary and took the mean n_eff over all parameters (mean(summary(stanfit)$summary[,'n_eff'])).
I also used get_elapsed_time() on the stanfit and calculated mean timing of the "sample" part over the chains (colMeans(get_elapsed_time(stanfit))[,'sample']).

I then simply divided n_eff with time.

These are the results for the original multi-normal version (note separate values for models with different priors for Sigma):

Prior        n_eff/time

IW              38.7
SIW            3.90
SSIW          12.9
SSLKJ        0.537

And these are the results for the reparameterized version:

Prior        n_eff/time

IW              38.4
SIW            36.3
SSIW          34.0
SSLKJ        67.6

I hope this was what you were after and that I haven't made a fool of myself by getting this totally wrong ;-).
And again, I not sure the comparison is completely valid since I haven't had time to check that there is a complete all else equal relationship between the two model versions.
I can say that the chains look muuch better after reparameterizing and there are basically no warnings etc produced for all prior versions above except the IW which basically did not have any problems in the first place.
 
/Martin

Hi stan users,

I am working on a multi-response poisson model (counts of a number of bird species are dependent on a set of predictors through species specific coefficients/parameters) and am currently trying to optimize the code to get rid of divergent transitions etc. and to speed up the analysis. Among other things I follow the suggestions in the manual about vectorizing probability functions and vectorization through matrix operations.

Just for future reference, reparameterization is not the same as (code) optimization. 

Before really getting into code optimization, you must make sure your model is fitting correctly. It's good practice to write the best code you can, but there's almost no point in trying to make the wrong thing go fast. You'll just get the wrong answer faster. (I can easily construct a Stan program that's really fast that doesn't do the right thing.)

I've seen improvements in multiple orders of magnitude with a reparameterization (remember, we don't care about wall time--we care about n_eff / time). With code optimization, you get percentage improvements: squeaking a 10% improvement is a big win (n_eff doesn't change, but time does).

 
The multi_normal probability functions (all versions including the cholesky variant which I am using) in Stan apparently can handle the argument Mu (location) as well as  the declared variable (left of the tilde) being an array of vectors while the scale (Sigma) is entered as a matrix. Thus, to vectorize the multi_normal sampling statement I can enter (in the model block) something like

 
loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L);

where loglambda and Mu are both N length arrays of R length vectors and L is the cholesky decomposed Sigma (matrix[R,R]) with N being the number of sites in my data and R being the number of species. I can hence vectorize the whole sampling statement and do not need to loop through my sites like this:

for (n in 1:N) {
        loglambda[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu[n], L);
}

However. I need to form Mu which is the predicted location(mean) and is dependent on the combination of my design matrix X (N by K (K=number of predictors + intercept)) and a matrix of species specific coefficients Beta (K by R). I can do this in an efficient way (says the manual) using matrix algebra:

Mu=X*Beta;

But this produces a matrix Mu (N by R) which is not (as far as I know) what multi_normal_cholesky() want. So an alternative is to use a loop to produce Mu in the right format (an N length array of R length vectors) by declaring X and Mu like:

row_vector[K] X[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...
row_vector[R] Mu[N];  // need to be row_vector to conform to the matrix algebra in the loop...

keeping Beta as a matrix[K, R] and looping through the sites (N):

for(n in 1:N){
        Mu[n] = X[n]*Beta; // Mu[n] is a row_vector of length R
      } 

But then I am not using the vectorization through matrix operations technique to the fullest?

My question is then: Is there an efficient way to "transform"(reshape) a matrix (matrix[N,R] Mu) to an array (vector[R] Mu[N]) such that it would be possible to have:

Mu=X*Beta;
"some reshaping function efficiently turning the matrix[N,R] Mu to the array vector[R] Mu[N]"
loglambda  ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu, L); 

Or is the looping step above a minor cost in terms of efficiency such that a reshaping function would not improve anything? Are there other solutions?


NB: this won't help with divergent transitions.

In general, loops are fast, expressions involving parameters are what matters -- both in number and complexity.
Vectorization of probability distribution functions not only cut down the number of expressions, but it also caches the reusable terms in a smart way.

For your problem, code speed is going to depend on size, but my guess is that this is the fastest to the slowest (in descriptions, not code):
1. Mu = X*Beta;
    use a for loop to assign cols to Mu_array
    loglambda ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Mu_array, L);

2. use a for loop to assign Mu_array
    loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu_array, L)

3. Use a loop for loglambda ~ multi_normal_choleskey(Mu, L)

My guess is that 1 and 2 are going to be comparable in speed and 3 is going to be the worst performance.



Daniel

P.S. I just saw that you posted. I'll take a read. Sorry, started this in the morning and was in a meeting before I could finish. 

    
 

I'd really appreciate any input on this

Sincerely,
Martin

Bob,
Thanks for the link. I'll take a closer look.

LKJ(eta<1) might apparently mitigate this but then I've seen claims that the LKJ sampler might be less stable and I haven't as yet experimented with it myself.
I am supposed to draw some ecological inferences from my analyses too and maybe not delve too far into statistics...ecology is after all my subject,  statistics is supposed to be one of my tools. 

Thanks for  all input given by all of you.

/Martin

When making such comparisons you have to be very careful with
your evaluations.  Different priors choices can affect not only sampling
speed and posterior inferences, but also the ability to fit the model
accurately at all.  Wishart and Inverse-Wishart not only imply odd
distributions for the correlations but they induce nasty posteriors that
frustrate accurate fitting, leading to the kinds of problems you see
here.  

So before comparing speed/efficiency or posteriors, you have to
validate that you’re getting a reasonable value.  This requires all
of the tricks — running multiple chains and checking Rhat, 
checking all of the HMC diagnostics like divergences and
the E-BFMI, and fitting simulated data and confirming that you
can recover the true values.  If you can’t do all of these then
the model can’t be fit with your sampler, and you can’t even
move onto the next step.

Lots of comparisons have been compromised by neglected
this step, which is especially important when Gibbs samplers are 
involved!

I am supposed to draw some ecological inferences from my analyses too and maybe not delve too far into statistics...ecology is after all my subject,  statistics is supposed to be one of my tools. 

Thanks for  all input given by all of you.

We don't recommend Wisharts. They're conjugate, which is
convenient when you're doing Gibbs, but Stan doesn't rely
on conjugacy.  For some motivation, see:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/

The only measure of efficiency we care about is n_eff/time (or its inverse).
Because n_eff tells us how many effectively independent draws you have,
which is the "size" of your sample --- errors in expectation calculations are
governed by 1 / sqrt(n_eff).

That will vary by parameter, though, so it's tricky when there are
lots of quantity of interests to compare.

- Bob

Den torsdag 8 december 2016 kl. 21:20:36 UTC+1 skrev Bob Carpenter:
We don't recommend Wisharts. They're conjugate, which is
convenient when you're doing Gibbs, but Stan doesn't rely
on conjugacy.  For some motivation, see:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/

The only measure of efficiency we care about is n_eff/time (or its inverse).
Because n_eff tells us how many effectively independent draws you have,
which is the "size" of your sample --- errors in expectation calculations are
governed by 1 / sqrt(n_eff).

That will vary by parameter, though, so it's tricky when there are
lots of quantity of interests to compare.

- Bob

involved!

We don't recommend Wisharts. They're conjugate, which is
convenient when you're doing Gibbs, but Stan doesn't rely
on conjugacy.  For some motivation, see:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/

The only measure of efficiency we care about is n_eff/time (or its inverse).
Because n_eff tells us how many effectively independent draws you have,
which is the "size" of your sample --- errors in expectation calculations are
governed by 1 / sqrt(n_eff).

That will vary by parameter, though, so it's tricky when there are
lots of quantity of interests to compare.

Of course, if my model cannot recover the true parameters of a simulated dataset I know it is not a good model. E_BFMI <- function(stanfit){
  nsamp <- dim(stanfit)[1]
  pars <- get_sampler_params(stanfit, inc_warmup=F)
  lapply(pars, function(x){
        deltaE <- x[1:nsamp-1, 'energy__'] - x[2:nsamp, 'energy__']
        margE <- x[,'energy__'] - mean(x[, 'energy__'])
        numer <- sum(deltaE^2)
        denom <- sum(margE^2)
        numer/denom
  })
}
